FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (Third Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards after the draft finalized by 
the Ceramicware Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 


This standard was first published in 1964 and was subsequently revised in 1975 and 2004 with a view to 
providing a commonly agreed terminology and definitions relating to ceramicware industry. Keeping in view the 
development of a variety of new methods and products in the field of ceramics, the committee responsible for 
the preparation of this standard decided to revise it and incorporate new terms and definitions which have come 
into use in this industry and trade. 


The composition of the technical committee responsible for formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 


In the formulation of this standard, due weightage has been given to bring about coordination among standards 
and practices prevailing in different countries in addition to relating it to the practices in the field in this 
country. This has been met by deriving assistance from publication C 242-15 ‘Standard terminology of ceramic 
whitewares and related products’, issued by the American Society for Testing and Materials, USA. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


Indian Standard 


GLOSSARY OF TERMS RELATING TO 
CERAMICWARE 


( Third Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


This standard covers the terms and definitions relating 
to ceramicware and related products. 


2 TERMS AND DEFINITIONS 


2.1 Absorption — The relationship of the mass of 
water absorbed by a ceramic specimen, subjected to 
prescribed immersion procedure, to the mass of the dry 
specimen, expressed in percent. 


2.2 Alumina Porcelain — A vitreous ceramic 
whiteware for technical application in which alumina 
(A1,0,) is the essential crystalline phase. 


2.3 Alumina Whiteware — Any ceramic whiteware 
in which alumina (A1,O,) is the essential crystalline 
phase. 


2.4 Artware — Ceramicware made principally for 
decorative purposes. 


2.5 Attritor — A type of grinding mill in which 
particles are moved by an impeller, attached to a central 
shaft. A churning action takes place while in operation, 
and size of the particles reduce by colliding with one 
another and/or grinding media. 


2.6 Ball Clay — A secondary clay, commonly 
characterized by the presence of organic matter, high 
plasticity, high dry strength, long vitrification range, 
and a light colour when fired. 


2.7 Ball Milling — A method of grinding and mixing 
materials, with or without liquid, in a rotating cylinder 
or conical mill partially filled with grinding media. 


2.8 Basalt Ware — A black unglazed vitreous 
ceramicware having the appearance of basalt rock. 


2.9 Belleek China — A highly translucent whiteware 
composed of a body containing a significant amount 
of frit and normally having a lustre glaze (produced 
commercially at Belleek, Ireland). 


2.10 Bentonite — A highly plastic clay containing 
extremely fine particles of volcanic origin, consisting 
mainly of montmorillonite; capable of taking up 


water rapidly and swelling to four to five times its 
dry volume. It has low fusion point and burns into a 
coloured product. 


2.11 Binders — Substances used for the purpose of 
cementing particles and for increasing the unfired 
mechanical strength of ceramic coatings or body and 
which may be expelled during firing. 


2.12 Bisque — An unglazed ceramicware fired 
to achieve sufficient mechanical strength at lower 
temperature (650° to 950°C). 


2.13 Bisque Fire — The process of firing ceramicware 
prior to glazing. 


2.14 Blister — A raised portion of the surface 
protruding not more than 1 mm above the surface 
and not greater than 3 mm in its maximum dimension 
developed during firing. 


2.15 Blistering — The development of a defect of 
enclosed or broken macroscopic vesicles or bubbles in 
a body, or in a glaze or other coating during firing. 


2.16 Blunging — The wet process of dispersion of 
agglomerates to fines, blending, or suspending ceramic 
materials in liquid medium by agitation. 


2.17 Body — The structural portion of a ceramic 
article, or the material or mixture from which it is 
made. 


2.18 Bone Ash — Calcined bone consisting essentially 
of calcium phosphate. 


2.19 Bone China — A white translucent porcelain 
made from a ceramic body containing a minimum of 
25 percent bone ash as the chief fluxing material. 


2.20 Bright Glaze — A colourless or coloured ceramic 
glaze having high gloss. 


2.21 Bubble — A raised portion of the surface or a sand 
speck not more than | mm in its maximum dimension. 


2.22 Calcine — A ceramic material or mixture fired 
to less than fusion for use as a constituent in a ceramic 
composition. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


2.23 Casting — Forming ceramicware by introducing a 
body slip into a porous mould which absorbs sufficient 
water from the slip to produce a semi-rigid (leather 
hard) article. 


2.24 Casting, Drain (Hollow Casting) — See ‘Drain 
Casting’. 


2.25 Casting, Solid — See ‘Solid Casting’. 
2.26 Casting, Tape — See ‘Tape Casting’. 


2.27 Ceramic Colour — Inorganic oxides or prepared 
mixtures used for obtaining colour decoration on fired 
ceramicware, or making coloured glazes. 


2.28 Ceramic Frit — Frit having ceramic composition 
to produce protective coating, bonding or fluxing of 
ceramic product. 


2.29 Ceramic Mosaic Tile — An unglazed tile formed 
by either the dust pressed or plastic method, usually 
6 to 9 mm thick and having a facial area of less than 
39 cm? and usually mounted on sheets approximately 
60 cm x 30 cm to facilitate setting. Ceramic mosaic tile 
may be of either porcelain or natural clay composition 
and may be either plain or with an abrasive mixture 
throughout. 


2.30 Ceramic Paste — A French term synonymous 
with ‘ceramic body’. 


2.31 Ceramic Process — The production of articles 
or coatings from essentially inorganic, non-metallic 
materials, the article or coating being made permanent 
and suitable for utilitarian and decorative purposes by 
the action of heat at temperatures sufficient to cause 
sintering, solid-state reactions, bonding or conversion 
partially or wholly to the glassy state. 


2.32 Ceramics — A class of brittle, inorganic, 
nonmetallic materials produced by high-temperature 
processing. The term covers glass, refractories, enamels, 
whiteware, etc. Also a generic term applied to the art or 
technique of producing articles by a ceramic process. 


2.33 Ceramicware — A glazed or unglazed fired ware 
made of ceramic materials characterized by its brittle 
nature. 


2.34 Cermets — A fired composite containing ceramic 
and metallic ingredients, and having the desired 
properties of both. 


2.35 Chamot — Refractory clay which has been 
specially fired and crushed for use as a non-plastic 
component of a refractory batch. It is usually made by 
calcining a refractory clay. 


2.36 Chemical Porcelain — Vitreous ceramicware 
used for storing, transporting, heating or reaction of 
chemicals. 


2.37 China — A glazed or unglazed vitreous ceramic 
whiteware used for non-technical purposes. This term 
designates such products as dinnerware, sanitaryware, 
and artware when they are vitreous. 


2.38 China, Belleek — See ‘Belleek China’. 
2.39 China, Bone — See ‘Bone China’. 
2.40 China Clay — See ‘Kaolin’. 

2.41 China, Hotel — See ‘Hotel China’. 


2.42 China Process — The method of producing glazed 
ware by which the ceramic body is fired to maturity, 
following which the glaze is applied and matured by 
firing at a lower temperature. 


2.43 China Sanitaryware (Sanitary Plumbing 
Fixtures) — Glazed, vitrified whiteware fixtures 
having a sanitary service function (see also Vitreous 
Sanitaryvvare). 


2.44 China, Semivitreous — See “Semivitreous 


China”. 
2.45 China, Vitreous — See “Vitreous China”. 


2.46 Chipping — Breaking off of chips from the edge 
of a glazed ceramicware. 


2.47 Clay — A natural mineral aggregate, consisting 
essentially of hydrous aluminium silicates. It is 
plastic when sufficiently wetted, rigid when dried en 
masse, and vitrified when fired to a sufficiently high 
temperature. 


2.48 Clay, Ball — See ‘Ball Clay’. 
2.49 Clay, China — See ‘Kaolin’. 
2.50 Clay, Fire — See ‘Fire Clay’. 
2.51 Clay, Primary (Residual) — See ‘Primary Clay’. 


2.52 Clay Secondary (Sedimentary) — See 


‘Secondary Clay’. 


2.53 Clayware — Any article made of clay with or 
without glaze and with or without the addition of other 
ingredients like feldspar and quartz. 


2.54 Clear Glaze — A colourless or coloured 
transparent ceramic glaze. 


2.55 Comminution — The process of reduction of 
particle size with attendant increase in surface area and 
population of particles usually by grinding, milling or 
pulverizing. 


2.56 Cordierite Porcelain — A vitreous ceramic 
whiteware for technical application in which cordierite 
(2MgO, 2 AI,O,.5SiO,) is the essential crystalline 
phase. 


2.57 Cordierite Whiteware — Any ceramic whiteware 
in which cordierite (2MgO, 2ALO,.5SiO,) is the 
essential crystalline phase. 


2.58 Covering Power — The ability of a glaze to 
uniformly and completely cover the surface of the fired 
ware. 


2.59 Crawling — A parting and contraction of the glaze 
on the surface of ceramicware during drying or firing, 
resulting in unglazed areas bordered by coalesced 
glaze. 


2.60 Crazing (or Craze) — The hair like cracking 
which occurs in fired glazes or other ceramic coatings 
due to critical tensile stresses. 


2.61 Crystalline Glaze — A glaze containing 
macroscopic crystals. 


2.62 De-airing — The process of removing entrapped 
air, or absorbed air from a mass or slurry, usually by 
application of a vacuum. 


2.63 Decorated — Adorned, embellished, or made 
more attractive by means of colour or surface detail. 


2.64 Decoration Firing — The process of firing 
ceramic or metallic decoration on the surface of glazed 
ceramicware. 


2.65 Decoration — See “Decoration, Inglaze’; 
‘Decoration, Overglaze’; and ‘Decoration, Underglaze’. 


2.66 Decoration, Inglaze — A ceramic decoration 
applied on the surface of an unfired glaze and matured 
with the glaze. 


2.67 Decoration, Monochrome — See ‘Monochrome 
Decoration’. 


2.68 Decoration, Overglaze — A ceramic or metallic 
decoration applied and fired on the previously glazed 
surface of ceramicware. 


2.69 Decoration, Polychrome — See ‘Polychrome 
Decoration’. 


2.70 Decoration, Underglaze — A ceramic decoration 
applied directly on the surface of ceramicware and 
subsequently covered with a transparent glaze. 


2.71 Deflocculate — To separate agglomerates in a 
slurry by chemical and physical means to achieve and 
maintain particle-to-particle separation. 


2.72 Deflocculant — A substance used for 
de-agglomeration and dispersion of particles (usually 
very fine). 


2.73 Deformation Eutectic — The composition vvithin 
a system of two or more components which on heating 


IS 2781 : 2020 


under specified conditions develop sufficient liquid to 
cause deformation at the minimum temperature. 


2.74 Delft Ware — A calcareous earthenware having 
an opaque white glaze and monochrome overglaze 
decoration (originated in Delft, Holland). 


2.75 Dilatometer/ry — An instrument/method used 
for measuring changes in linear dimensions of a sample 
with heating/cooling. 


2.76 Dinnerware — Ceramic whiteware made in a 
given pattern and in a full line of articles comprising a 
dinner service. 


2.77 Discolouration — A defect due to the appearance 
of an undesirable colour in a finished product or due to 
fading of desired colour. 


2.78 Dispersant — See ‘Deflocculant’. 


2.79 Doctor Blade — A blade usually kept vertical 
over a flat bed, so as to maintain a definite, pre-defined 
gap between the edge of the blade and the flat bed. 
Forcing a fluid medium through the doctor blade results 
in formation of uniform layer of the fluid, used for tape 
casting and screen printing processes. 


2.80 Dolomite — The double carbonate of lime and 
magnesia having the general formula CaMg(CO,).,. 


2.81 Drain Casting — Forming ceramicware by 
introducing a body slip into an open porous mould, 
and draining off the remaining slip when the cast has 
reached the desired thickness. 


2.82 Dry Edging — Rough edges and corners of glazed 
ceramicware due to insufficient glaze coating. 


2.83 Drying — Removal by evaporation, of 
uncombined vvater or other volatile substance from a 
ceramic ravv material or product, usually expedited by 
low-temperature heating and flow of air. 


2.84 Dry Mix — The method of preparation of a 
ceramic body wherein the constituents are blended dry, 
following which liquid may be added as required for 
subsequent processing. 


2.85 Dry Pressing — Forming ceramicware in 
dies from powdered or granular material by direct 
pressure. 


2.86 Dry Process — See ‘Dry Mix’. 


2.87 Dunt — A hair-line fracture extending through or 
into the body of the ware. 


2.88 Dunting — A hair-line crack that occurs both in 
the body and glaze in fired ceramicware during cooling 
and storage. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


2.89 Earthenware — A glazed or unglazed nonvitreous 
ceramicware. 


2.90 Earthenware, Sanitaryware — Sanitaryware 
having earthenware body structure showing water 
absorption not exceeding 15 percent. 


2.91 Egg-Shell Finish — Dead or flat finish appeared 
to be undeveloped glaze slightly matt in appearance 
or a semi-glazed finish exhibiting numerous very fine 
pinholes and non-glossy appearance. 


2.92 Egg Shelling — The texture of a fired glaze 
similar in appearance to the surface of an egg shell. 


2.93 Electrical Porcelain — Vitrified whiteware 
having an electrical insulating function. 


2.94 Embossed — A decoration in relief or excised on 
the ware surface. 


2.95 Engobe — A decoration white or coloured slip 
coating applied to a ceramicware for imparting colour, 
opacity or other characteristics, and subsequently 
covered with a glaze and fired. 


2.96 Equilibrium Eutectic — The composition within 
any system of two or more crystalline phases which 
melts completely at the minimum temperature, or the 
temperature at which such a composition melts. 


2.97 Eutectic — See ‘Eutectic, Deformation’ and 
‘Eutectic, Equilibrium’. 


2.98 Eutectic, Deformation — See ‘Deformation 
Eutectic’. 


2.99 Eutectic, Equilibrium — See ‘Equilibrium 
Eutectic’. 


2.100 Exposed Body — Portions of glazed ceramicware, 
more than 1.5 mm in diameter, from where glaze has 
been removed due to defective workmanship. 


2.101 Extrusion - A process of pressurizing a dough like 
mixture of solid particles, prepared with a combination 
of various liquid as well as solid additives, through an 
orifice (die) to give a defined shape. 


2.102 Faience — A decorated glazed earthenware. 


2.103 Faience Mosaics — Faience tiles, that are less 
than 39 cm? in facial area, usually 8 to 9 mm thick, and 
usually mounted to facilitate installation. 


2.104 Faience Tile — Glazed or unglazed tile, generally 
made by the plastic process, showing characteristic 
variations in the face, edges, and glaze that give a 
hand-crafted, non-mechanical, decorative effect. 


2.105 Faience Ware — Formerly a decorated 
earthenware with an opaque glaze, but currently 


designating a decorated earthenware having a 
transparent glaze. 


2.106 Feathering — Superficial crystallization of the 
glaze surface. 


2.107 Felspar, Feldspar — A mineral aggregate 
consisting chiefly of microcline, albite and/or anorthite. 


2.108 Fire — See ‘Fire, Bisque’; ‘Fire, Decorating’; 
‘Fire, Glost’ and ‘Fire, Single’. 


2.109 Fire, Bisque — See ‘Bisque Fire’. 


2.110 Firecheck — A fine shallow crack in the body 
not covered with glaze. 


2.111 Fire Clay — A secondary clay which does not 
show any incipient fusion below 1 580°C. 


2.112 Fire, Glost — The process of kiln-firing bisque 
ware to which glaze has been applied. 


2.113 Fire, Single — The process of maturing an unfired 
ceramic body and its glaze in one firing operation. 


2.114 Firing — The controlled heat treatment of 
ceramicware in a kiln or furnace, during the process of 
manufacture, to develop the desired properties. 


2.115 Firing Curve — A diagram or table showing the 
time and temperature planned or experienced by ware 
going through a firing operation. 


2.116 Firing Cycle — The time required for one 
complete firing operation (cold-to-cold). 


2.117 Firing, Decoration — See ‘Decoration Firing’. 


2.118 Firing Range — The range of firing temperature 
within which a ceramic composition develops 
properties which render it commercially useful. 


2.119 Flatware — Articles having an internal depth not 
exceeding 25 mm as measured from the lowest internal 
point to the horizontal plane passing through the point 
of overflow. 


2.120 Flowing — Excessive movement of the molten 
glaze due to its being less viscous at the temperature of 
firing, resulting in collection of glaze at the foot of the 
article or spreading of colour decoration. 


2.121 Flux — A substance that promotes fusion in a 
given ceramic mixture. 


2.122 Foodware — A flatware and hollowware used 
in the preparation, serving or storage of food and 
beverages. 


2.123 Forming — The shaping or moulding of 
ceramicware. 


2.124 Forsterite Porcelain — A vitreous ceramic 
whiteware for technical application in which forsterite 
(2MgO.SiO),) is the essential crystalline phase. 


2.125 Forsterite Whiteware — Any ceramic 
whiteware in which forsterite (2MgO.SiO,) is the 
essential crystalline phase. 


2.126 Frit — It is an intermediate product formed 
by quenching in water or between water-cooled 
rolls, a mixture of inorganic materials from the 
molten state. It may be partially crystalline. It is used 
for providing a protective coating in admixture with 
various additives on different ceramics, glassware and 
metal. 


2.127 Fritted Glaze — A glaze in which a part or all 
the constituents are prefused. 


2.128 Fusion — The process of melting; usually the 
result of interaction of two or more materials. 


2.129 Glaze — A ceramic coating matured to glassy 
state on a formed ceramic article, or the material or 
mixture from which the coating is made. 


2.130 Glaze, Bright — See ‘Bright Glaze’. 
2.131 Glaze, Clear — See ‘Clear Glaze’. 


2.132 Glazed Ceramic Mosaic Tile — Ceramic 
mosaic tile with glazed faces. 


2.133 Glazed Interior Tile — A glazed tile with 
a body that is suitable for interior use and which is 
usually non-vitreous, and is not required or expected 
to withstand excessive impact or be subject to freezing 
and thawing conditions. 


2.134 Glazed Tile — Tile with a fused impervious 
facial finish composed of ceramic materials, fused 
into the body of the tile which may be a nonvitreous, 
semivitreous, vitreous, or impervious body. The glazed 
surface may be clean, white or coloured. 


2.135 Glazed Tile, Extra Duty Glaze — Tile with a 
durable glaze that is suitable for light duty floors and all 
other surfaces on interiors where there is no excessive 
abrasion or impact. 


2.136 Glaze Fit — The stress relationship between the 
glaze and body of a fired ceramic product. 


2.137 Glaze, Fritted — See ‘Fritted Glaze’. 
2.138 Glaze, Matt — See “Matt Glaze’. 

2.139 Glaze, Opaque — See ‘Opaque Glaze’. 
2.140 Glaze, Raw — See ‘Raw Glaze’. 

2.141 Glaze, Salt — See ‘Salt Glaze’. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


2.142 Glaze, Semi-Matt — See ‘Semi-Matt Glaze’. 
2.143 Glaze, Slip— See ‘Slip Glaze’. 

2.144 Glaze, Vellum — See ‘Vellum Glaze’. 

2.145 Glost Fire — See ‘Fire, Glost’. 


2.146 Granulation — A process of deliberately 
adhering fine primary particles in a powder to give rise 
to larger multi-particle entities, termed as granules, 
with the help of bonds created by external additives 
(binder) and/or pressure. 


2.147 Grinding Media — Media/means used for 
particle size reduction by crushing/grinding particles 
in a mill. 


2.148 Hard Porcelain — A completely vitrified 
translucent, generally vvhite, hard body vvhich does not 
vitrify below 1 350°C. 


2.149 Healing Povver — The ability of a glaze to heal 
surface blemishes during firing. 


2.150 Hollowware — Articles having an internal 
depth greater than 25 mm as measured from the lowest 
internal point to the horizontal plane passing through 
the point of overflow. 


2.151 Hollowware, Large — Hollowware with a 
capacity of 1.1 1to 51. 


2.152 Hollowware, Small — Hollowware with a 
capacity less than 1.11. 


2.153 Hotel China — A non-translucent ware made 
of dense, strong, white body of vitreous china type, 
biscuited at a high temperature and later glost fired at a 
relatively lower temperature. 


2.154 Hot Pressing — A jigger process wherein a 
heated profile, tool or plunger forms the plastic body 
by direct pressure. 


2.155 Impervious — The degree of vitrification 
evidenced visually by complete resistance to dye 
penetration. 


2.156 Incised — Decorated by cutting or indenting the 
ware surface. 


2.157 Inglaze Decoration — See “Decoration, Inglaze’. 


2.158 Ironstone Ware (Stone China, White 
GraniteWare) — Historic terms for a durable English 
earthenware. 


2.159 Jasper Ware — A vitreous, opaque, coloured 
unglazed ceramicware having white or contrasting 
relief decorations and containing a substantial amount 
of barites, originally developed by Josiah Wedgwood. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


2.160 Jiggering — Forming ceramicware from a 
plastic body by differential rotation of a profile tool and 
mould, the mould having the contour of one surface of 
the ware and the profile tool that of the other surface. 


2.161 Kaolin (China Clay) — A refractory clay 
consisting essentially of minerals of the kaolin group 
and which fires to a white or nearly white colour. 


2.162 Kiln Support Marks — Unglazed patches left 
on the ware purposely as also pin or line marks from 
where the glaze is removed on account of support given 
to the ware during firing. 


2.163 Knockings — The oversize residue obtained in 
screening a ceramic slip. 


2.164 Limestone — A sedimentary carbonate rock, 
composed chiefly of calcite (CaCO,), but sometimes 
containing appreciable dolomite. 


2.165 Loss on Ignition — The percent loss in weight 
of a material on being calcined at a temperature 
sufficiently high, and for a time long enough, to achieve 
constant weight without melting, expressed as a percent 
of the initial weight of the dry material (without free 
moisture). 


2.166 Lubricant — Additive used for reducing 
frictional forces encountered during the particulate 
materials processing, for example, between die walls 
and powders, between powder particles. 


2.167 Magnesia — Magnesium oxide (MgO), calcined 
or hard burnt as periclase loosely applied also to 
the hydrate Mg(OH),, and made synthetically from 
seawater or brine, or (impure) from magnesite. 


2.168 Majolica — Formerly an earthenware with an 
opaque lustre glaze and overglaze coloured decorations, 
but currently designating any decorated earthenware 
having an opaque glaze. 


2.169 Masking Power — The ability of a fired glaze to 
mask visually the body on which it is applied. 


2.170 Matt Glaze — A colourless or coloured ceramic 
glaze having low gloss. 


2.171 Maturing Range — The time-temperature 
range within which a ceramic body, glaze or other 
composition may be fired to yield specified properties. 


2.172 Melt — To change a solid into a liquid by the 
application of heat; or the liquid resulting from such 
action. 


2.173 Mineralizer — A processing additive that 
promotes either the recrystallization or the partial 
fusion or sintering of certain mineral or ceramic 
materials, often facilitating the desired conversion at a 
lower temperature. 


2.174 Moisture Expansion — An increase in 
dimension or bulk volume of a ceramic article caused 
by reaction with water or water vapour. 
NOTE — This reaction may occur in time at atmospheric 
temperature and pressure, but is expedited by exposure of the 


article to water or water vapour at elevated temperatures and 
pressures. 


2.175 Monochrome Decoration — A single colour 
decoration. 


2.176 Mullite Porcelain — A vitreous ceramic 
whiteware for technical application in which mullite 
(3ALO,.2S1O,) is the essential crystalline phase. 


2.177 Mullite Whiteware — Any ceramic whiteware 
in which mullite (3ALO,.2Si0,) is the essential 
crystalline phase. 


2.178 Microstructure —Very fine scale structure of a 
material, observed under a microscope. 


2.179 Natural Clay Tile — A tile made by either the 
dust-pressed method or the plastic method, from clays 
that produce a dense body having a distinctive, slightly 
textured appearance. 


2.180 Nepheline Syenite — A mineral aggregate 
consisting chiefly of albite, microcline and nephelite, 
each in significant amount. 


2.181 Nonvitreous (Nonvitrified) — That degree 
of vitrification evidenced by relatively high water 
absorption. 


NOTE — The term ‘nonvitreous’ generally signifies more than 
10 percent water absorption. 


2.182 Opaque Glaze — A nontransparent coloured or 
white glaze. 


2.183 Orange Peel — A pitted texture of a fired glaze 
resembling the rough surface of orange peel. 


2.184 Oven Ware — Ceramic whiteware for use over 
culinary oven. 


2.185 Overglaze Decoration — See ‘Decoration, 
Overglaze’. 


2.186 Particle — A minute quantity or fragment of 
matter whose size and shape depend on the forces of 
cohesion. It is usually only a single crystal or a unit of 
matter with a specific gravity approximating that of a 
single crystal. 


2.187 Particle Size Distribution — A profile of the 
sizes of particles contained in a material in which the 
quantities must be expressed on some basis which may 
be total number, total surface, or total weight or volume 
of the particles in the material. 


2.188 Paste Ceramic — See ‘Ceramic Paste’. 


2.189 Pate Dure (Hard Paste) — A French term 
designating ceramic whitewares fired at relatively high 
temperatures. 


2.190 Pate Tendre (Soft Paste) — A French term 
designating ceramic whitewares fired at relatively low 
temperatures. 


2.191 Pavers — Unglazed porcelain or natural 
clay tile formed by the dust-pressed method and 
similar to ceramic mosaics in composition and physical 
properties but relatively thicker with 15 cm” or more of 
facial area. 


2.192 Peeling — See ‘Shivering’. 


2.193 Pinholes — Imperfections in the surface of a 
ceramic body or glaze resembling pin pricks less than 
1.5 mm in diameter. 


2.194 Placing Sand — Silica sand, ground kyanite or 
saggar grog used as placing sand for placing unglazed 
article in the saggar before loading in the kiln to save 
the article from sticking to the saggar as also to avoid 
distortion of shape during firing. 


2.195 Plasticizer — Additive used in ceramic 
processing to impart plasticity to the dough mixture. 


2.196 Plastic Pressing — See ‘Pressing, Wet’. 


2.197 Polishing Mark — A spot where some minor 
blemish has been ground off and the surface polished, 
the area of the spot not exceeding the area of a 10 mm 
diameter circle. 


2.198 Polyehrome Decoration — A multicolour 
decoration. 


2.199 Polymer —A substance comprising of molecules 
of high molecular mass, formed by joining of repeating 
structural units on a large scale. For example, plastics, 
resins etc. 


2.200 Porcelain — A glazed or unglazed vitreous 
whiteware. This term designates such products as 
electrical, chemical, mechanical, structural, thermal 
and tablewares when they are vitreous. 


2.201 Porcelain, Alumina — See ‘Alumina Porcelain’. 


2.202 Porcelain, Chemical — See ‘Chemical 
Porcelain’. 
2.203 Porcelain, Cordierite — See “Cordierite 
Porcelain’. 
2.204 Porcelain, Electrical — See ‘Electrical 
Porcelain’. 
2.205 Porcelain, Forsterite — See ‘Forsterite 


Porcelain’. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


2.206 Porcelain, Hard — See “Hard Porcelain’. 
2.207 Porcelain, Mullite — See ‘Mullite Porcelain’. 


2.208 Porcelain Process — The method of producing 
glazed ware by which a ceramic body and glaze are 
matured together in the same firing operation. 


2.209 Porcelain, Semi — See ‘Semiporcelain’. 
2.210 Porcelain, Soft — See ‘Soft Porcelain’. 
2.211 Porcelain, Steatite — See “Steatite Porcelain’. 


2.212 Porcelain Tile — A ceramic mosaic tile or paver 
that is generally made by the dust-pressed method, 
of a composition resulting in a tile that is dense, 
fine-grained, and smooth with sharply formed face, 
usually impervious. Colours of the porcelain tile are 
usually of a clear, luminous type or granular blend 
thereof. 


2.213 Porcelain, Titania — See ‘Titania Porcelain’. 
2.214 Porcelain, Zircon — See ‘Zircon Porcelain’. 


2.215 Pore Former — A substance which decomposes 
and escapes the mixture during heating, thus leaving 
the final product with pores. 


2.216 Pore Size and Distribution — The size and 
distribution of pores in a ceramic body (green or 
sintered). 


2.217 Porosity, Apparent — The volume fraction of 
all pores, voids, and channels within a solid mass that 
are interconnected with each other and communicate 
with the external surface, and thus are measurable by 
gas or liquid penetration. 


2.218 Porosity, Closed — The volume fraction of 
all pores within a solid mass that are closed off by 
surrounding solid and, hence, are inaccessible to each 
other and to the external surface. They, thus, are not 
detectable by gas or liquid penetration. 


2.219 Porosity, Connected — The volume fraction of 
all pores, voids and channels within a solid mass that 
are interconnected with each other. 


2.220 Porosity, Open — See ‘Porosity, Apparent’. 


2.221 Pottery — All fired ceramic wares that contain 
clay when formed, except technical, structural, and 
refractory products. 


2.222 Pottery Square — A square area of dimensions 
50 mm x 50 mm selected on the ware for examining 
visual defects. 


2.223 Pressing, Dry — See ‘Dry Pressing’. 
2.224 Pressing, Hot — See ‘Hot Pressing’. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


2.225 Pressing, Wet (Plastic Pressing) — Forming 
ceramicware in dies from a plastic body by direct 
pressure. 


2.226 Primary Clay (Residual Clay) — A clay which 
remains geologically at its place of formation. 


2.227 Process, Ceramic — See ‘Ceramic Process’. 
2.228 Process, China — See ‘China Process’. 
2.229 Process, Dry — See ‘Dry Mix’. 


2.230 Process, Wet (Slip Process) — The method of 
preparation of a ceramic body wherein the constituents 
are blended in sufficient liquid to produce a fluid 
suspension for use as such or for subsequent processing. 


2.231 Pyrophyllite — A hydrated aluminium silicate 
mineral of the theoretical composition Al,O,.4S1O.. 
H,O, having physical properties in the raw state 
resembling mineral talc. 


2.232 Quarry Tile — Unglazed tile, usually 39 cm? 
or more in surface area and 10 to 20 mm in thickness, 
made by the extrusion process from natural clay or 
shales. 


2.233 Raw Glaze — A glaze compounded primarily 
from raw constituents, that is, containing no prefused 
materials. 


2.234 Rockingham Ware — A semivitreous ware or 
earthenware having a brown or mottled brown bright 
glaze (originated in England on the estate of the 
Marquis of Rockingham). 


2.235 Saggar — A fire clay container for keeping 
glazed ware for firing to protect it from smoke, dust 
and dirt of the kiln atmosphere. 


2.236 Salt Glaze — A glaze produced by the reaction, 
at elevated temperature, between the ceramic body 
surface and salt fumes produced in the kiln atmosphere. 


2.237 Secondary Clay (Sedimentary Clay) — A clay 
which has been geologically transported from its place 
of formation. 


2.238 Semi-matt Glaze — A colourless or coloured 
glaze having moderate gloss. 


2.239 Semiporcelain — A trade term designating 
semivitreous dinnerware. 


2.240 Semivitreous China — A development of 
earthenware biscuited at a high temperature and glost 
fired at a relatively lower temperature and having water 
absorption between 3 and 7 percent by mass. 


2.241 Semivitreous (Semivitrified) — That degree of 
vitrification evidenced by a moderate or intermediate 
water absorption. 


NOTE — The term ‘semivitreous’ generally signifies 0.5 to 
10.0 percent water absorption. 


2.242 Ship and Galley Tile — A special quarry tile 
having an indented pattern on the face to produce an 
antislip effect. 


2.243 Shivering (Peeling) — The splintering which 
occurs in fired glazes or other ceramic coatings due to 
critical compressive stresses. 


2.244 Shrinkage — The irreversible reduction in 
dimensions of a green body during ceramic processing; 
may be observed at different stages in the process, 
namely, drying, heating etc. 


2.245 Sieve — A standard wire mesh or screen, 
especially when used in graded sets to determine the 
mesh size or particulate size distribution of particulate 
or granular solids. 


2.246 Sieve Analysis — The particle size distribution 
of a particulate of granular solid or sample thereof, 
when determined by weight percent passage through, 
or retention on, a graded set of sieves. 


2.247 Silica (SiO,) — The common oxide of silicon 
usually found naturally as quartz or in complex 
combination with other elements as silicates. 


2.248 Single Fire — See ‘Fire, Single’. 


2.249 Sinter — A ceramic material or mixture fired to 
less than complete fusion, resulting in a coherent mass, 
or the process involved. 


2.250 Slip Coating — A ceramic material or mixture 
other than a glaze, applied to a ceramic body and fired to 
maturity required to develop specified characteristics. 


2.251 Slip Glaze — A glaze consisting primarily of a 
readily fusible clay or silt. 


2.252 Slip Process — See ‘Process, Wet’. 


2.253 Slip (Slurry) — A suspension of ceramic 
materials in a liquid with or without addition of 
deflocculants. 


2.254 Slip, Vitreous — See ‘Vitreous Slip’. 

2.255 Slurry — See ‘Slip (Slurry)’. 

2.256 Smelt (n) — A specific batch or lot of frit. 
2.257 Smelt (v) — The act of melting a batch of frit. 


2.258 Soft Porcelain — A completely vitrified, more 
or less translucent, white or ivory body fired below 
1250°C. 


2.259 Solid Casting — Forming ceramicware by 
introducing a body slip into a porous mould which 
usually consists of two major sections, one section 


forming the contour of the outside and the other forming 
the contour of the inside of the ware and allowing a 
solid cast to form between the two mould faces. 


2.260 Special Purpose Tile — A tile, either glazed or 
unglazed, made to meet or to have specific physical 
design or appearance characteristics, such as size, 
thickness, shape, colour, or decoration; keys or lugs 
on back or sides, special resistance to staining, frost, 
alkalis, acids, thermal shock, physical impact, high 
coefficient of friction, or electrical properties. 


2.261 Speck — An area of contrasting colour less than 
1 mm maximum dimension. Specks less than 0.25 mm 
maximum dimension do not constitute a defect unless 
sufficient in number to form a discolouration. 


2.262 Spitout — A glaze defect developed in the 
decorating kiln, due to evolution of minute gas bubbles 
from body or glaze. 


2.263 Spot — A discoloured portion of the surface not 
exceeding 3 mm in its maximum dimension. 


2.264 Steatite Porcelain — A vitreous ceramic 
whiteware for technical application in which 
magnesium metasilicate (MgO.SiO,) is the essential 
crystalline phase. 


2.265 Steatite (Talc) — Massive talc or the 
pulverized product thereof having the general formula 
3Mg0.4SiO..H.O. 


2.266 Steatite VVhitevvare — Any ceramic vvhitevvare 
in which magnesium metasilicate (MgO.SiO,) is the 
essential crystalline phase. 


2.267 Stoneware — A semivitreous ceramicware 
of fine texture, usually off-white in colour and made 
primarily from non-refractory clays. 


2.268 Stoneware Clays — Plastic clays having low 
shrinkage and burning into dense off-white body at 
about 1 250°C. 


2.269 Tableware — All utensils and decorative articles 
made of ceramics used on the table for meal service. 


2.270 Tape casting — A process of casting a dough like 
mixture of solid particles, prepared with a combination 
of various liquid as well as solid additives, through a 
doctor blade. 


2.271 Terracota — A porous, red clay ware. 


2.272 Terra Sigillata — A porous red clay ware 
characterized by embossed decorations of the same 
colour and a satin-like unglazed surface (originated on 
the island of Samos). 


2.273 Thermal Shock — A condition of stress brought 
about by a large temperature difference across a body 
or glaze. 


IS 2781 : 2020 


2.274 Thermogravimetry — An analytical technique 
to monitor and record the change in mass of a sample 
(usually a small representative sample, in a few 
milligram quantity), as a function of temperature. 


2.275 Tile — A ceramic surfacing unit, usually 
relatively thin in relation to facial area, made from 
clay or a mixture of clay and other ceramic materials, 
called the body of the tile, having either a ‘glazed’ 
or ‘unglazed’ face and fired above red heat in the 
course of manufacture to a temperature sufficiently 
high to produce specific physical properties and 
characteristics. 


2.276 Tile, Ceramic Mosaic — See ‘Ceramic Mosaic 
Tile’. 


2.277 Tile, Faience — See ‘Faience Tile’. 
2.278 Tile, Glazed — See ‘Glazed Tile’. 


2.279 Tile, Glazed, Ceramic Mosaic — See ‘Glazed 
Ceramic Mosaic Tile’. 


2.280 Tile, Glazed, Extra Duty Glaze — See ‘Glazed 
Tile, Extra Duty Glaze’. 


2.281 Tile, Glazed, Interior — See ‘Glazed Interior 
Tile’. 


2.282 Tile, Porcelain — See ‘Porcelain Tile’. 


2.283 Tile, Ship and Galley — See ‘Ship and Galley 
Tile’. 


2.284 Tile, Special Purpose — See ‘Special Purpose 
Tile’. 


2.285 Tile, Unglazed — See ‘Unglazed Tile’. 


2.286 Titania — Titanium dioxide corresponding to 
molecular formula TiO,,. 


2.287 Titania Porcelain — A vitreous ceramic 
whiteware for technical application in which titania 
(TiO,) is the essential crystalline phase. 


2.288 Titania Whiteware — Any ceramic whiteware 
in which titania (TiO,) is the essential crystalline 
phase. 


2.289 Trimmers — Units of various shapes consisting 
of such items as bases, caps, corners, mouldings, 
angles, etc, necessary or desirable to make a complete 
installation and to achieve sanitary purposes as well as 
architectural design for all types of tile work. 


2.290 Underglazed Decoration — See ‘Decoration, 
Underglaze’. 


2.291 Unglazed Tile — A hard, dense tile of 
homogeneous composition throughout, deriving 
colour and texture from materials of which the body 
is made. The colours and characteristics of the tile 


IS 2781 : 2020 


are determined by the materials used in the body, the 
method of manufacture and the thermal treatment. 


2.292 Vellum Glaze — A semi-matt glaze having a 
satin-like appearance. 


2.293 Viscosity — The viscosity of a fluid is a measure 
of its resistance to gradual deformation by shear stress 
or tensile stress. 


2.294 Vitreous (Vitrified) That degree of 
vitrification evidenced by low water absorption (see 
also ‘Impervious’ and ‘Semivitreous’). 


NOTE — The term ‘vitreous’ generally signifies less than 
0.5 percent water absorption. 


2.295 Vitreous China — A while vitrified body 
biscuited at a high temperature and glost fired at 
a relatively lower temperature and having water 
absorption less than 0.5 percent by mass. 


NOTE — Vitreous china sanitaryware is fired only once. 


2.296 Vitreous Sanitaryware — A sanitaryvvare 
having a vitrified body structure showing water 
absorption not exceeding 0.5 percent. 


2.297 Vitreous Slip — A slip coating matured on a 
ceramic body, producing a vitrified surface. 


2.298 Vitrification — The progressive reduction in 
porosity of a ceramic composition as a result of heat 
treatment, or the process involved. 


2.299 Vitrification Range — The maturing range of a 
vitreous body. 


2.300 Ware, Art — See ‘Artware’. 

2.301 Ware, Basalt — See ‘Basalt Ware’. 

2.302 Ware, Clay — See “Clayvvare”. 

2.303 Ware, Cordierite — See ‘Cordierite Whiteware’. 
2.304 Ware, Ironstone — See ‘Ironstone Ware’. 
2.305 Ware, Jasper — See ‘Jasper Ware’. 

2.306 Ware, Oven — See ‘Oven Ware’. 

2.307 Ware, Rockingham — See ‘Rockingham Ware’. 


2.308 Ware, 
Sanitaryware’. 


Sanitary, China See ‘China 


2.309 Ware, Stone — See ‘Stoneware’. 
2.310 Ware, Yellow — See ‘Yellow Ware’. 


2.311 Warpage — Distortion of original shape during 
the manufacturing process. 


10 


2.312 Wavy Finish — A defect in the glaze finish 
having the appearance of numerous runs in the glaze, 
irregular or mottled. 


2.313 Wet Pressing — See ‘Pressing Wet’. 
2.314 Wet Process — See “Process Wet’. 


2.315 White Ware — A fired ware consisting of a 
glazed or unglazed ceramic body which is commonly 
white and of fine texture. This term designates such 
products as china, porcelain, semivitreous ware and 
earthenware. 


2.316 Whiteware, 
whiteware’. 


Alumina See ‘Alumina 


2.317 Whiteware, Cordierite — See ‘Cordierite 
Whiteware’. 


2.318 Whiteware, 
Whiteware’. 


Forsterite — See ‘Forsterite 


2.319 Whiteware, Mullite — See ‘Mullite Whiteware’. 
2.320 Whiteware, Steatite — See ‘Steatite Whiteware’. 
2.321 Whiteware, Titania — See ‘Titania Whiteware’. 
2.322 Whiteware, Zircon — See ‘Zircon Whiteware’. 


2.323 Whiting — Calcium carbonate powder of high 
purity. 


2.324 Wollastonite A calcium metasilicatc 
mineral with the formula CaSiO, containing 
theoretically 48.3 percent lime (CaO) and 51.7 percent 
silica (SiO,), occurring in acicular masses of elongated 
triclinic crystals, usually white or pale gray. 


2.325 Yellow Ware — A yellow semivitreous ware or 
an earthenware with a colourless, clear glaze. 


2.326 Zeta Potential — The charge that develops at 
the interface between a solid surface of a suspended 
particle and its liquid medium. Used as a key indicator 
for the stability of colloidal solutions. The magnitude 
of the zeta potential indicates the degree of electrostatic 
repulsion between adjacent, similarly charged particles 
in a suspension. 


2.327 Zircon — The mineral zircon (zirconium silicate) 
corresponding to molecular formula ZrO..SiO.. 


2.328 Zircon Porcelain — A vitreous ceramic 
whiteware for technical application in which zircon 
(ZrO,.SiO,) is the essential crystalline phase. 


2.329 Zircon Whiteware — Any ceramic whiteware 
in which zircon (ZrO,.SiO,) is the essential crystalline 
phase.

Bureau of Indian Standards 


BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 to promote harmonious 
development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and attending to 
connected matters in the country. 


Copyright 


BIS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced in any form without 
the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of implementing the 
standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. Enquiries relating to 
copyright be addressed to the Director (Publications), BIS. 


Review of Indian Standards 


Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 
‘BIS Catalogue’ and ‘Standards: Monthly Additions’. 


This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc No.: CHD 09 (12612).
